extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; poets and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria for judging or composing English poetic description and style (exemplified by Chaucer and Spenser) — what makes poetic imagery, pathos, allegory, and versification effective. Focus is on qualities of language, imagination, tone, and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gusto / local truth and freshness in natural description
rubrics_metrics.description: Chaucer's descriptions of natural scenery possess 'gusto'. They have a local truth and freshness, which gives the very feeling of the air, the coolness or moisture of the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make inanimate objects participate in the feeling of the scene so they 'render back the sentiment of the speaker's mind.' Example: the opening of the Flower and the Leaf where the coolness of the arbour, early time, birds, and scent produce an appearance like recollection of an actual scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evocative imagery combining beauty and abstract power
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination of a poet brings objects before us 'clothed in beauty, formidable in the sense of abstract power.' There is a 'pleasing awe' in terrible yet beautiful description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use images that are simultaneously beautiful and formidable to evoke awe (example: Chaucer's tame leon and leopart whose claws are pared but whose presence is powerful). Balance attractiveness with an impression of strength or sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in nature / reliance on subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature is the soul of art: there is a strength and simplicity in the imagination that reposes entirely on nature, that nothing else can supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on natural observation and fidelity to the subject rather than artifice; such trust yields sustained sentiment and authentic feeling (e.g., Chaucer's depiction of grief, patience, faith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple, deep, sustained pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Chaucer 'has more of this deep, internal, sustained sentiment' and 'in depth of simple pathos, and intensity of conception, never swerving from his subject'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for concentrated, internally sustained feeling rather than melodrama; keep the sentiment consistent and focused on the subject (examples: Griselda's calm heroic patience; the child's martyrdom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected rapture and flowery sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'no affected rapture, no flowery sentiment' where true poetic delight is natural and unforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid artificial exuberance or overwrought ornamentation; prefer ebullitions of natural delight 'welling out of the heart' rather than contrived rapture (antipattern: forced, mannered exultation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification: strength, harmony, and reading practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Chaucer's versification has considerable strength and harmony; apparent deficiencies often arise from later changes in pronunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading older verse, adopt historically-informed pronunciation (Hazlitt's rule: pronounce the final 'e' in Chaucer) to recover intended cadence and harmony. Appreciate versification as partly mechanical but potent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain distinctness of tone (do not confound styles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spenser (and Chaucer) could 'pass at will from grave to gay, from lively to severe'; but they 'never confounded the two styles together.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be able to shift tone when appropriate, yet keep tones distinct within a piece; avoid mixing comic and pathetic modes in a way that undermines each (allowed exception: the unconscious mixture found in nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry implies/suggests; painting describes the visible
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting describes what the object is in itself, poetry what it implies or suggests; moral impressions (Death, Night, Space) are essentially visionary and reside in the mind's eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dealing with abstract or moral subjects, prefer suggestion, insinuation, and visionary language over precise physical depiction. Resist the impulse to 'make a shadow as substantial as possible'—indistinctness can be a virtue in poetry where the invisible is to be evoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of abrupt, rapid gleams of description
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry can produce effects by 'a few abrupt and rapid gleams of description, touching, as it were with fire, the features and edges of a general mass of awful obscurity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing vast or awful subjects, employ brief, striking images rather than exhaustive detail. This creates a sense of the unformed and vast by lighting edges rather than outlining everything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent abstractions by being less definite
rubrics_metrics.description: The less definite, the less bodily the conception, the more vast, unformed, and unsubstantial, the nearer it approaches the omnipresent, lasting, universal principle (e.g., Death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-specific physicalization of moral or metaphysical concepts; allow vagueness and generality to suggest universality and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality, richness, and invention in subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Spenser 'has an originality, richness, and variety in his allegorical personages and fictions' which rivals ancient mythology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive personification and novel mythic material enrich poetry—value imaginative expansion of subject-matter and creation of fresh allegorical figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of beauty can outweigh truth — aesthetic impulse as guide
rubrics_metrics.description: For Spenser, 'the love of beauty, however, and not of truth, is the moving principle of his mind; and he is guided in his fantastic delineations by no rule but the impulse of an inexhaustible imagination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when aesthetic luxuriance or imaginative impulse is an authorial choice; this can produce sumptuous verse but may also sacrifice 'truth' or naturalness. Judge whether luxuriance serves the poem's aims or becomes mere affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory should not obscure comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to Spenser's allegory are misplaced: 'If they do not meddle with the allegory, the allegory will not meddle with them.' The allegory need not obstruct plain enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft allegory so that readers can enjoy the surface narrative and imagery without decoding every allegorical sign; intelligibility and immediate pictorial pleasure are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid, picturesque character-portraits and personifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Spenser's Procession of the Passions and the Mask of Cupid present clear, often grotesque or comic, portraits (e.g., Gluttony, Lechery) with sensory detail and moral description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create allegorical figures with concrete, memorable traits (dress, gestures, emblematic objects) so they operate as effective moral or satirical portraits (examples: Gluttony's swollen belly, Lechery on a bearded goat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Different kinds of pathos: remote sentimental vs immediate dramatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Spenser 'has not the pathos of immediate action or suffering' (dramatic pathos) but 'has all the pathos of sentiment and romance'—pathos of distant, imaginary distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which emotional register you aim for: immediate, dramatic involvement (as in tragedy) or romantic/distant sentiment (as in Spenser). Each is a legitimate mode; evaluate consistency and effectiveness accordingly.
